opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly one of the most interesting open problems in this space. I think there are a couple of different ways you can come at it.

One approach is the very explicit one: you have a physics engine, you have a simulator, and you try to bolt that onto your model or train against it. That gives you a lot of guarantees. You know objects won't pass through each other, you know gravity points down. But it's also brittle. Real-world physics is incredibly messy: cloth, fluids, deformable objects, people. Hand-engineering all of that doesn't really scale.

The other approach, which I think is where a lot of the excitement is right now, is to learn physics implicitly from data. If you look at large video models, they've picked up a surprising amount of intuitive physics just from watching enormous amounts of video. Things fall, water splashes, light reflects in mostly plausible ways. Nobody wrote down Newton's laws for them. That's a really powerful signal that scale and data can get you a long way.

But I think the interesting thing about working in 3D is that you get a better substrate for that learning. When your representation is fundamentally three-dimensional, things like object permanence, consistent geometry, and occlusion come much more naturally. In a purely 2D pixel model, an object can kind of melt away when the camera turns, because there's no underlying world state forcing it to persist. Once you have an explicit 3D world, a lot of physical consistency gets baked into the structure of the representation itself.

So my view is that the long-term answer is probably some hybrid. You want strong 3D structure as an inductive bias. You want to learn as much as possible from large-scale data, because the world is too complicated to hand-specify. And then maybe for certain applications, like robotics, where you really need precise dynamics, you lean on more classical simulation where it makes sense. We're still pretty early in figuring out the right balance, and that's part of what makes it such a fun area to work on.

r001.rationale: The response proposes using a physics engine or simulator and mentions gravity, but it does not say to supervise the model on physical forces.

r002.rationale: The response says video models can learn intuitive physics from data, but it does not connect that learning to an end-to-end broader prediction task that requires physics for accurate predictions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, and honestly my view has shifted over the last few years. The old-school approach, and the one I grew up with academically, is that you hand-engineer the physics. You write down a simulator, you've got rigid body dynamics, you've got a renderer, and the learning problem is sort of fitting parameters inside that structure. And that works great when your world fits the assumptions of your simulator. The problem is the real world mostly doesn't. Cloth, hair, water, deformable stuff, people, all the messy things that make the world interesting are exactly the things that are hardest to write a simulator for.

So the bet we're making at World Labs, and I think the bet a lot of the field is making now, is that you don't teach physics explicitly. You let the model learn it the same way video models have started to learn it, by seeing a ton of data where physical consistency is the thing that explains what happens next. If you watch enough footage of objects falling, bouncing, occluding each other, the cheapest way for the model to predict the next frame is to actually internalize something like gravity and contact and persistence. It doesn't need the equations, it needs the regularities.

The nuance, though, and this is where I think the 3D part matters, is that pure video models learn physics in a very entangled way. The geometry, the lighting, the motion, the camera, all of that is smeared together in pixel space. And that makes it hard to ask the model simple questions like, if I move this object, where does it end up. So what we care about is giving the model enough structure that the world it produces is an actual spatial thing. There's a persistent scene, objects have locations, the camera is something you can move independently. You don't hard-code the physics, but you do give the model a representation where physics has somewhere clean to live. Then the dynamics can be learned on top of that, and when they're learned on top of a real 3D substrate, they tend to be a lot more consistent and controllable.

The honest answer is that we're early on the dynamics side. Static 3D generation has gotten really good really fast. Getting things to move in ways that are physically believable over long horizons, and that you can intervene on, that's still the frontier. My intuition is it'll fall to the same recipe, more data and the right inductive biases, but the inductive bias I believe in isn't a physics engine. It's just that the world is three-dimensional and persistent, and everything else is learned.

r001.rationale: The response argues against explicitly teaching or hard-coding physics; it does not propose supervision on physical forces.

r002.rationale: It says that learning physical regularities from video helps the model predict what happens next, and that predicting accurately can lead it to internalize gravity, contact, and persistence.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is whether the model is learning what the world looks like or how the world behaves. You can generate something that looks convincing in a single frame, but once an object moves or interacts with something else, you need a much more coherent model of what’s going on.

One way to approach that is through prediction: given what’s happened so far, and perhaps an action, predict what happens next. That creates pressure to learn things like objects persisting when they’re occluded, or collisions changing how objects move. You don’t necessarily have to encode all of that as explicit equations, but you do need data where those interactions are observable.

The tricky part is figuring out whether the model learned a general rule or just a familiar visual pattern. I’d want to test it by changing the setup—moving an object, changing an initial condition, taking a different action—and seeing whether the consequences remain consistent. That’s a stronger test of understanding physics than just producing a plausible-looking video.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning from observable interactions but does not propose explicitly supervising the model on physical forces.

r002.rationale: It says prediction can pressure a model to learn persistence and collision behavior, but does not clearly state that the model is trained end to end on a broader prediction task.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting question is how much physics you need to put into the model explicitly, versus how much it can learn from observing the world. A video contains a lot of evidence about physics: objects fall, things collide, something goes behind another object and then comes back. But predicting what those events look like isn’t necessarily the same as understanding the dynamics that produced them.

One way to push on that distinction is to let the model take actions. If I push this object, what happens? If I push it harder, what changes? Now you need to capture something about the underlying state of the world, because your predictions have to remain consistent across different interventions.

I don’t think that necessarily means we have to build a classical physics engine into every model. But we do need training data and evaluations that reward consistent dynamics over time. A beautiful five-second video is one thing. A world you can interact with, where objects keep behaving coherently, is a much stronger test.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether physics must be built into a model, but does not propose explicitly supervising the model on physical forces.

r002.rationale: It says models can learn from observations and that interactive predictions need consistent underlying state, but does not state that end-to-end training on a broader prediction task would implicitly teach physics because physics is needed for accurate predictions.
